name: Microneedling pen (electric)
lead: An electric microneedling pen is a motorised handheld device that drives a cartridge of fine needles rapidly up and down into the skin to create controlled micro-injuries. The body responds with a wound-healing cascade that people use to soften acne scars and stretch marks, refine texture and pores, and in some protocols to help even out pigmentation or support hair regrowth; it is a staple of skin and scar discussion in looksmaxxing forums, and the Dermapen is the best-known branded example.[2][3]

The pen is one form of collagen induction therapy, a family that also includes manual dermarollers and stamps. Compared with a roller, a pen moves its needles vertically with adjustable depth and speed, which manufacturers describe as giving more uniform channels with less lateral tearing.[3] Clinics offer pen microneedling alone, with topical serums, with platelet-rich plasma (PRP, sometimes marketed as a 'vampire facial'), or combined with radiofrequency, and consumers buy lower-cost pens and cartridges online.[2][13][20]

Dermatology research consists largely of small trials, many from single centres, that compare pen microneedling with peels or other treatments or use it to deliver topical products and PRP. A systematic review of 51 articles and 1,029 patients described microneedling as a relatively safe procedure,[1] while rare but notable adverse reactions have been reported, including granulomatous reactions in which motorized pens and topical vitamin C application were implicated in most published cases.[4] The US FDA lists microneedling devices authorised for facial acne scars, facial wrinkles and abdominal scars and describes treatment as performed by a trained provider;[19] the American Academy of Dermatology has documented risks of at-home pens and layered products.[20]

chain: Needles create controlled micro-injuries in the skin
Wound healing signals fibroblasts to produce new collagen and elastin
Scars, stretch marks and rough texture look smoother over a series of sessions
angle.text: People use pens to resurface acne scars, stretch marks and rough skin by triggering the skin's own repair response, typically as a course of sessions spaced weeks apart. The same channels are used to help topical products or PRP reach deeper, which is why pens are paired with serums in clinics and online routines.

card.summary: Motorised needle pen for collagen induction; decent small-trial support for scars and texture, but rare reactions and depth/hygiene issues at home.
card.note: Rare granulomatous reactions reported, mostly with motorized pens and topical vitamin C.

quick.overview:
An electric microneedling pen rapidly punctures the skin with fine disposable needles to trigger repair. It is used for acne scars, texture, stretch marks and sometimes hair or pigment problems, and is a staple of looksmax skincare talk.

Small randomized studies report improvement in acne scars, often better when combined with peels or other agents, but many trials are small and from single centres, and long-term data are limited.
quick.mechanism: The needles create micro-injuries that start wound healing, release growth factors and stimulate collagen and elastin production, and the channels may help topical products penetrate.
quick.risks: A systematic review described microneedling as relatively safe overall. Rare granulomatous reactions have been reported, with motorized pens and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases. Forum discussions of deep home settings are personal reports rather than clinical guidance.

paras: Pen devices hold a disposable needle cartridge and move the needles in and out of the skin at adjustable speed and depth. Their vertical stamping motion is contrasted by manufacturers with the angled entry of rolling devices.[3] According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, the Dermapen was introduced in 2010 by the Australian company DermapenWorld, whose chief executive is named as Stene Marshall, and the flagship Dermapen 4 launched in April 2018 with a 16-needle, 33-gauge cartridge and depth adjustable up to 3 mm; the company claims millions of treatments in dozens of countries. That account relies largely on manufacturer-sourced material.[3]

The same account describes a consumer model, Dermapen HOME, with shallower depths of 0.1 to 0.5 mm and recommended use every 7 to 10 days, and notes contraindications such as active infection, bleeding disorders, recent isotretinoin use, keloid tendency and pregnancy.[3] Clinics also use radiofrequency (RF) microneedling devices, in which the needles deliver energy into the skin; forum members sometimes suggest paying for professional RF microneedling instead of deep needling at home.[12][19]

Cheaper generic pens and cartridges are sold to consumers online through large marketplaces, and the American Academy of Dermatology notes that some electronic pens are marketed widely despite a lack of standardised oversight and authorised distribution; looksmax.org discussions compare such pens with clinical devices.[12][13][20]

Microneedling in its roller form was described in the dermatology literature in the 2000s as a simple option for atrophic acne scars. A 2009 study of 37 patients treated with a roller at monthly intervals found 72.2 percent had an excellent clinician-graded response, with the author noting limits such as no control group and two-month follow-up.[21] In 2012 Liebl and Kloth proposed that microneedles stimulate skin cells by briefly disrupting the skin's natural electrical fields, while stating that much of this was speculative.[22]

Powered pens followed. DermapenWorld says it introduced the first automated microneedling pen in 2010, and later generations added features such as depth calibration and anti-contamination systems.[3] Wikipedia notes that microneedling has been used for scarring, acne and hair loss and that research on combinations such as PRP is still developing.[23]

Public attention to safety rose in April 2024 when, as summarised on Wikipedia, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported HIV diagnoses among patients of an Albuquerque spa that offered PRP microneedling ('vampire facials') without infection-control training; health officials warned such services in non-medical settings could spread bloodborne infections.[23]

Reviews describe microneedling as creating micro-injuries that start the inflammation, proliferation and remodelling phases of wound healing, activate platelet growth factors and stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and elastin.[2] Because the skin's outer layer closes quickly, redness typically settles within a couple of days, according to one proposal of the mechanism.[22] The puncture channels are also reported to increase penetration of topical agents,[2] which is why pens are used to deliver PRP, tranexamic acid, vitamin C, drugs for vitiligo and growth factors in studies and in forum routines.[5][6][7][9]

Acne scars are the best-studied use: rolling, boxcar and shallow scars are described as responding better than deep ice-pick scars in the roller literature.[21] Stretch marks, fine lines, large pores and uneven texture are common targets, along with pigment disorders such as melasma, where the needling is used to deliver agents such as PRP or tranexamic acid.[5][6][7]

For hair, pens are studied and used alongside topical minoxidil or PRP for androgenetic alopecia, and T Nation members report using a Dermapen weekly alongside Rogaine after stopping testosterone therapy, with others suggesting it as part of a hair-loss routine.[11][12][17][18][23] One forum poster describes planning a routine using his own blood, comparing the result to a 'vampire lifting'.[12]

Practitioners in clinics typically use topical anaesthetic, a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, and a sterile single-use cartridge, followed by sun protection and a bland moisturiser; the AAD advises dermatologists to counsel against aggressive needle depths at home and to avoid highly active products on disrupted skin.[20][21]

A randomized comparison of 60 patients with atrophic acne scars found that a pen-based microneedling group improved more than a Jessner's peel group, and that combining the two gave the best results.[5] Other studies compared a pen with glycolic acid peels for acne scars,[8] assessed two microneedle devices on opposite sides of the face,[9] and compared microneedling with plasma regeneration for stretch marks.[10]

Pens have also been studied as delivery tools in melasma with platelet-rich plasma (a 23-patient study compared Dermapen delivery with microinjection)[6] or tranexamic acid versus vitamin C,[7] in vitiligo with topical drugs,[14][15][16] and in androgenetic alopecia with platelet-rich plasma.[11] Many of these are small, regionally conducted studies, and a review lists conditions where benefit has been reported while noting the heterogeneity of methods.[2]

Human trials have studied pen-type microneedling for acne scars,[5][8][9] stretch marks,[10] melasma,[6][7] vitiligo[14][15][16] and androgenetic alopecia,[11] mostly as small comparative or randomized studies. A systematic review of 51 articles covering 1,029 patients evaluated safety across device types,[1] and an older uncontrolled study of roller microneedling in 37 patients reported mostly excellent responses for mild to moderate atrophic acne scars at two months.[21] Long-term durability data are limited.

A systematic review of microneedling adverse effects covering roller, stamp, pen and radiofrequency devices examined published complications, describing the procedure as relatively safe.[1] Rare granulomatous reactions have been described in 15 patients, with motorized pen use and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases; the authors note that these can be treatment-resistant.[4]

Because needles break the skin barrier, products applied afterward can enter deeper tissue than intended. The AAD lists foreign-body granulomas after non-sterile or non-intradermal products (vitamin C serums, PDRN, oils, exosomes), infection or abscess from reused needles or contaminated bottles, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation especially in skin of colour, barrier damage, scarring from excessive depth or dull needles, contact dermatitis, and flares of rosacea; its review of TikTok found users applying many such products during treatment.[20]

The FDA says certain microneedling devices are authorised for facial acne scars, facial wrinkles and abdominal scars in patients aged 22 and over through De Novo or 510(k) pathways, that some cosmetic-only products may not be medical devices, and in October 2025 issued a safety communication on certain uses of radiofrequency microneedling.[19]

On looksmax.org, members ask what maximum needle depth is appropriate on the face for a pen, with replies describing depths of 1 to 2 mm, intervals between sessions, and waiting periods before reintroducing actives such as vitamin C, tretinoin and acids; some replies suggest paying for professional radiofrequency microneedling instead.[12] Other threads discuss cheap generic pens, with one user reporting more than two years of use.[13] These are personal reports, not clinical advice.

T Nation threads mention Dermapen use in hair-loss routines, a 2018 thread titled around increased testosterone absorption after dermarolling, and another poster's mention of copper peptides and needling for scar and stretch-mark routines.[17][18][24][25]

lore.intro: Electric pens are discussed on looksmax.org as a home or low-cost route to skin renewal, with attention to needle depth and device choice, and in T Nation threads as an add-on to hair-loss routines.[12][13][17][18]

claims.claim: Deeper needle depth gives better results, with limits around 1.5 mm.
claims.believers: Posters say deeper is generally better but that 1.5-2 mm should be used rarely, risks scarring, and needs longer breaks from actives.[12]
claims.experts: Published studies use varied depths and devices; reviews describe serious adverse effects, including granulomatous reactions, as uncommon, while the AAD cautions against aggressive depths at home.[1][4][20]

claims.claim: Cheap generic pens work as well as branded ones.
claims.believers: One poster reports a generic pen working well after two years of heavy use, while another recommends a different type.[13]
claims.experts: A study compared two microneedle devices on opposite sides of the face for acne scars;[9] no study of low-cost consumer pens against branded devices was found, and the AAD notes variable oversight of online-sold pens.[20]

claims.claim: Needling lets serums such as vitamin C work much deeper.
claims.believers: Forum routines add vitamin C, tretinoin and acids at set intervals after needling and treat the channels as a delivery route.[12]
claims.experts: Reviews report the channels increase penetration,[2] but a systematic review of granulomatous reactions implicated topical vitamin C with motorized pens in most cases,[4] and the AAD advises avoiding actives on disrupted skin.[20]

claims.claim: Microneedling with PRP or one's own blood rejuvenates skin.
claims.believers: A poster describes using his own blood for anti-ageing and compares 1 mm depth to a 'vampire lifting'.[12]
claims.experts: Trials of PRP delivered with a pen exist in melasma and hair loss, mostly small;[6][11] Wikipedia notes efficacy of PRP combinations awaits further studies and that non-medical settings have been linked to bloodborne infection concerns.[23]

claims.claim: A pen is a cheap way to treat acne scars at home.
claims.believers: Members present generic pens as a budget alternative to clinic treatment.[13]
claims.experts: Randomized trials of pen microneedling in clinics report improvement in acne scars, especially combined with peels;[5][8] the FDA describes authorised treatment as done by a provider and the AAD warns of home risks.[19][20]

claims.claim: Microneedling helps hair regrowth alongside minoxidil.
claims.believers: A T Nation member reports weekly Dermapen sessions alongside Rogaine after stopping testosterone therapy, and another suggests needling with other hair-loss treatments.[17][18]
claims.experts: A small pilot study and a trial of Dermapen PRP application in androgenetic alopecia are published, and Wikipedia reports a pilot in which needling plus minoxidil outperformed minoxidil alone.[11][23]
